question: How much organ meat should I feed my dog?
answer: The well-known '10% rule' really only needs to apply to liver, because liver stores fat-soluble vitamin A, which can accumulate to excess — so cap liver at around 5–10% of the diet. It's worth feeding, though, because liver is the best source of vitamin A, B12, folate, iron, and copper. Other organs don't carry the same accumulation risk: kidney only needs caution in very high amounts, and spleen is rich enough that too much can cause loose stools. Variety across organs gives the broadest nutrition.
source: Common Sense Dog — Organs, TCVM & Lipoma pack

question: Is liver good for dogs and how much is safe?
answer: Liver is one of the most nutrient-dense foods you can feed — it's the top source of vitamin A, B12, folate, iron, and copper. The only caution is that vitamin A is fat-soluble and accumulates, so keep liver to roughly 5–10% of the overall diet rather than feeding it in large amounts daily. At that level it's a powerful whole-food multivitamin. This is the one organ where the 10% cap genuinely matters.

question: Is heart a good food for dogs?
answer: Heart is one of the best ingredients you can feed — and despite being an organ, it behaves like a muscle meat with no accumulation risk, so you can feed it generously, even as a primary protein. It's exceptionally rich in taurine and CoQ10 (both vital for heart health), plus B vitamins, iron, and zinc. This is 'like feeds like' in action: heart literally supports the heart. It's affordable and an easy, high-value addition to most bowls.

question: What is green tripe and why is it good for dogs?
answer: Green tripe is the raw, unbleached stomach lining of grazing animals, and it's a holistic favorite because it naturally supplies probiotics and digestive enzymes along with a balanced protein and a good fatty-acid profile. It supports gut health and digestion in a whole-food form, and most dogs love it. It can be fed in higher quantities without the cautions that apply to liver. The only real downside is the strong smell — a sign of how alive and unprocessed it is.

question: What does 'like feeds like' mean in dog nutrition?
answer: It's a core idea from Traditional Chinese Veterinary Medicine (TCVM): feeding a specific organ supports that same organ in your dog. Heart feeds the heart (taurine, CoQ10), liver feeds the liver (B12, iron), and kidney supports the kidneys (selenium). The whole-food, organ-specific nutrients are thought to nourish and strengthen the matching system. It's a practical reason to include a variety of organ meats rather than relying on muscle meat alone.

question: What are warming and cooling proteins in TCVM for dogs?
answer: In TCVM, foods carry an energetic 'temperature.' Cooling proteins include duck, fish/salmon, rabbit, and venison; neutral proteins include beef, turkey, and pork; warming proteins include chicken and lamb. A dog that runs hot does better on a cooling-leaning diet, while a dog that runs cold benefits from warming proteins. The goal is an overall trend, not a perfect every-meal rule — you're nudging the body toward balance.

question: How do I know if my dog 'runs hot' in TCVM terms?
answer: Signs a dog runs hot include excessive panting, seeking out cool surfaces to lie on, red eyes, and always seeming thirsty. These dogs tend to do better with cooling proteins like duck, fish, rabbit, and venison, and you'd limit warming proteins like chicken and lamb — being strict about that mainly when active heat signs show up. Fish and salmon are especially good picks because they're both cooling and the best source of anti-inflammatory omega-3s. It's about steering the overall diet cooler, not obsessing over every meal.

question: What causes lipomas (fatty tumors) in dogs?
answer: While conventional advice often calls lipomas harmless and random, the holistic view is that they're driven by chronic low-grade inflammation and a poor diet — the same root that underlies many modern dog diseases. High-carb, ultra-processed food spikes insulin and promotes fat storage, and inflammatory omega-6 oils keep the body inflamed. So lipomas are seen less as bad luck and more as a visible signal of internal imbalance. Address the diet and inflammation, and you address the cause rather than just the lump.
source: Common Sense Dog — Organs, TCVM & Lipoma pack

question: What foods should I avoid for a dog with lipomas?
answer: Cut the inflammatory and high-insulin drivers: high-omega-6 oils (sunflower, safflower, corn, soybean, generic 'vegetable oil'), corn/wheat/soy, peas, lentils, chickpeas, and canola, plus synthetic preservatives (BHA, BHT, ethoxyquin), artificial colors, added sugar, and high-carb foods generally. Many gently cooked brands quietly fail here because they use pea protein, canola, and synthetic vitamins. Reading the label matters — the goal is to remove the fuel for inflammation and fat storage.
source: Common Sense Dog — Organs, TCVM & Lipoma pack

question: What should I feed to help manage my dog's lipomas?
answer: Lean into an anti-inflammatory, lower-carb, whole-food diet with a good omega ratio. Fish and salmon (cooling + rich omega-3s) and duck are great proteins, and a food with a near-balanced omega-6:3 ratio acts as an anti-inflammatory anchor. Liver and kidney support detox, which matters if the dog is also on medications. Brands that avoid the inflammatory ingredients work for exactly that reason. Pair the diet with omega-3 supplementation and keep carbs modest.

question: Why are omega-6 vegetable oils bad for inflamed dogs?
answer: Oils like sunflower, safflower, corn, soybean, and generic vegetable oil are very high in omega-6 fatty acids, which in excess push the body toward inflammation. Most kibble already runs a badly skewed omega-6:3 ratio (often 15:1 to 30:1 versus a target of 5:1 or lower), and these oils make it worse. For any dog dealing with inflammation — lipomas, allergies, arthritis — reducing omega-6 and adding omega-3 (fish, salmon, fish oil) is one of the highest-impact diet changes you can make. It's about rebalancing the ratio, not eliminating fat.
source: Common Sense Dog — Organs, TCVM & Lipoma pack

question: Can kidney and spleen be fed to dogs?
answer: Yes. Kidney is a good source of B12, selenium, iron, and zinc, and only needs caution in very high amounts. Spleen is nutrient-rich (a good source of iron) but can cause loose stools if you overdo it, so feed it in moderation. Neither carries the strict vitamin-A accumulation concern that liver does. Rotating a variety of organs — heart, liver, kidney, spleen, tripe — gives your dog the broadest whole-food nutrition.
source: Common Sense Dog — Organs, TCVM & Lipoma pack
